python_igraph.notes: Rust port wins decisively at the smallest scales (triangle ~2x, ring-6 weighted ~7x) where Python/C-FFI overhead dominates upstream. On the karate / ring-of-cliques exemplars the Rust port is currently ~3-5x slower than python-igraph's native C walktrap; this is the expected gap for a v1 implementation that pays in two places: (1) the inner-loop random-walk probability vectors are dense Vec<f64> instead of the sparse Map<u32, f64> the C reference switches to once communities exceed a threshold, and (2) the per-merge Δσ recomputation walks all shared neighbours rather than reusing pre-computed pair triangles. Both are accuracy-preserving optimisations and tracked for an alpha.3 follow-up.

notes: Hot loop is the agglomerative merge: pop highest -Δσ from a hand-rolled binary min-heap, refine the entry's Δσ via the triangle formula or chain lower bound, then push back if not yet exact. The lazy-refine pattern avoids recomputing every entry per merge.

Internal graph stores a synthesized self-loop per vertex (weight = mean incident edge weight, or 1.0 if isolated) — same fix as upstream issue #2043. This makes the L2 distance between probability vectors invariant to isolated/leaf-vertex pathology.
Probability representation: full Vec<f64> sized to vcount. The C reference switches between full and sparse Map<u32, f64> at runtime; we may follow up in alpha.3.
Modularity trajectory matches the C `community_walktrap.out` reference fixture to ~1e-15 on the 6-ring weighted case (last value -5.55e-17 vs zapsmall(0)); conformance tolerance is 1e-12.

Two-K5-bridge bench variance is wide because the merge order can flip-flop on tied Δσ rows; once communities polarise this stabilises. Karate variance is similarly wide for the same reason. Per-fixture warmup tightens the band but doesn't change the median.
